questions.q: Why can't "helpfulness" be hand-written as a reward function the way +1-per-timestep works for CartPole?
options: Because language models don't support reward functions at all
Because helpfulness is identical to response length
Because reward functions can only be written for discrete action spaces
Because helpfulness depends on the prompt, user intent, factual correctness, and tone simultaneously, with no fixed rule capturing the tradeoffs
questions.explain: Unlike a physics simulator's score, 'good text' depends on many interacting, context-dependent factors that resist being reduced to a simple formula.

questions.q: What happened when early approaches used hand-written heuristics (length penalties, keyword matching) as a reward for language model outputs?
options: They hit the same failure mode as the boat-racing agent — the policy learned to satisfy the heuristic without producing genuinely good text
They worked perfectly with no downsides
They eliminated the need for human annotators permanently
They required no training data at all
questions.explain: Hand-written heuristics are proxies, and the policy optimizer finds ways to score well on the proxy that don't match real quality — the same reward hacking pattern from lesson 33.

questions.q: What is a reward model (RM), formally?
options: A lookup table of pre-approved responses
A rule-based scorer with hand-tuned weights
A learned function r_θ(prompt, response) that outputs a scalar score, trained to predict which response a human would prefer
The same model as the language model being trained, with no separate weights
questions.explain: The reward model is typically a pretrained transformer with its output head replaced by a scalar regression head, trained on human preference comparisons.

questions.q: Why do both the InstructGPT paper and Anthropic's helpful-and-harmless paper use preference comparisons rather than asking annotators for absolute 1-10 ratings?
options: Comparisons require no human involvement
Absolute ratings cannot be stored digitally
Absolute ratings are faster to collect
Different annotators anchor absolute scales inconsistently, while "which response is better" is a much more consistent judgment to make
questions.explain: Comparative judgments are far more consistent across and within annotators than absolute scale ratings, and they're sufficient to train a usable reward model.

questions.q: Where does the reward model fit in the overall RLHF pipeline?
options: It replaces the language model entirely after training
It is only used to filter the pretraining corpus
It has no role once the language model is deployed to users
It stands in for a human reviewer during reinforcement learning, scoring the language model's generated responses to supply the reward signal an RL algorithm optimizes against
questions.explain: Once trained, the reward model substitutes for a human during RL: the policy generates a response, the reward model scores it, and that score is the reward signal (typically optimized with PPO).
